title: Nomura Report Finds AI Creating More Jobs in India Than It Cuts
excerpt: A new Nomura Holdings report describes India as 'ground zero' for AI's labor market impact, but says hiring driven by AI adoption is outpacing job losses across the country.
body:
• Nomura Holdings reports that AI-driven recruitment in India exceeds AI-related job losses
  • India is experiencing the "largest absolute impact" of AI across layoffs, hiring freezes, and new recruitment globally
  • Separate data shows AI hiring in India's IT sector rose 16% year-on-year in June, even as overall IT jobs fell 3%

A report by Nomura Holdings Inc. has found that AI is creating more jobs in India than it is eliminating, challenging the dominant narrative that artificial intelligence will be a net destroyer of employment in the country. The report describes India as experiencing the "largest absolute impact" of AI across layoffs, hiring freezes, and recruitment, given the country's vast workforce — but says the balance tilts toward job creation, according to the Times of India.

More Hiring Than Firing

According to the Nomura report, AI-driven recruitment continues to exceed job losses across India. The country's scale — with hundreds of millions in the labor force — means that both the disruptions and the opportunities created by AI are larger in absolute terms than in most other economies. But the net effect, according to Nomura, is positive: more roles are being created to build, deploy, and manage AI systems than are being eliminated through automation.

This aligns with a broader pattern visible in recent hiring data. AI hiring within India's IT sector rose 16% year-on-year in June, while overall IT job listings fell 3%, according to Naukri's monthly JobSpeak report cited by Reuters. Across 14 sectors, AI and machine learning jobs increased 25% during the same period.

"The divergence between AI and overall IT hiring is important because it shows where tech companies are still investing. AI is increasingly becoming a core capability area."

— Hitesh Oberoi, CEO of Info Edge (Naukri's parent company)

The Workforce Is Being Reshaped, Not Just Shrinking

The data points to a labor market being reorganized rather than simply contracting. Tata Consultancy Services, India's largest IT exporter, said last month that it expects IT companies to slow traditional hiring while moving toward having an equal number of employees and AI agents in its workforce. TCS cut more than 12,000 jobs last July, and its headcount fell by over 23,000 on a net basis in the fiscal year ended March 2026, according to Reuters.

At the same time, global IT firms are increasing their India headcount. Capgemini, Cognizant, and EPAM all grew their India employee base in calendar year 2025, seeing the country's talent pool as a competitive staffing solution for AI-related roles, according to Livemint.

Entry-Level Roles Feel the Pressure

A separate study by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER), supported by OpenAI, found that 55% of firms reported a decline in entry-level employment, while mid-level and senior-level staffing remained more stable. The study cautioned that this moderation in hiring reflects a slowdown in the pace of new recruitment rather than mass layoffs, and partly aligns with broader post-pandemic adjustments in the IT industry.

Across more than 1,900 business divisions surveyed, productivity gains from AI significantly outnumbered declines, suggesting generative AI is functioning more as a productivity tool than a direct substitute for workers.

What It Means for Indian Tech Workers

The findings carry direct implications for India's $315 billion IT industry and the millions of workers it employs. While routine, execution-heavy roles are increasingly moving to AI agents, the demand for specialized talent — in data, AI, cloud, and platform engineering — is growing. Companies are willing to pay 30-40% salary premiums for cybersecurity professionals with AI specialization, according to TeamLease Services.

For workers, the shift adds pressure to build AI-adjacent skills rather than wait for broad IT hiring to recover. The Nomura report suggests India's workforce isn't simply getting larger or smaller — it is being reshaped around the skills companies expect to need next.
nri_angle: Indian tech workers globally face a shifting landscape where AI skills command premium salaries, while traditional IT roles face automation pressure across the $315 billion industry.
